# Regularization and Geometry Constraints

Also called: Geometric Regularization, Depth Regularization, Frequency Regularization, Surface Priors

## Overview
Regularization and geometry constraints address the tendency of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to produce "floaters" (noisy, unstructured density clouds) and over-reconstructed artifacts by imposing physical or spectral consistency during optimization [S1, S2]. Unlike [Base 3DGS Optimization](7549-base-3d-gaussian-splatting.md) which relies solely on photometric loss, this family enforces constraints on the Gaussian shapes, positions, or frequency spectra to align the learned representation with geometric priors or spectral expectations [S1, S2]. It sets itself apart from [Physical Parameter Optimization](4111-physical-parameter-optimization.md) by focusing on structural coherence rather than physical plausibility of materials, and from [WildGaussians](6064-wildgaussians.md) by explicitly penalizing geometric deviations rather than just mitigating transient occlusions.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family modify the standard photometric loss $\mathcal{L}_{photometric}$ by adding a regularization term $\mathcal{L}_{reg}$:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{total} = \mathcal{L}_{photometric} + \lambda_{reg} \mathcal{L}_{reg}
$$
where $\lambda_{reg}$ is a weighting factor [S1, S2]. The core mechanism involves either:
1.  **Geometric Alignment:** Constraining Gaussian centers, opacities, or covariance matrices to align with external depth estimates, surface normals, or local surface geometry [S1, S2].
2.  **Spectral Consistency:** Constraining the frequency content of the rendered image to match the ground truth, preventing high-frequency noise or over-smoothing [S2].
3.  **Shape Regularization:** Forcing Gaussians to flatten into surfels or align with local normals to reduce floaters [S1, S2].

## Subtopics

### [Frequency Regularization](6130-frequency-regularization.md)
Frequency Regularization minimizes the discrepancy between the frequency spectrum (amplitude and phase) of rendered and ground truth images to alleviate over-reconstruction. It sets itself apart from [Smoothed 2D Supervision](7213-smoothed-2d-supervision.md) by operating in the Fourier domain rather than the spatial domain, and from [Hard and Soft Depth Regularization](9178-hard-and-soft-depth-regularization.md) by targeting spectral consistency rather than geometric depth alignment. Choose this when over-reconstruction or high-frequency noise is prevalent.

### [Smoothed 2D Supervision](7213-smoothed-2d-supervision.md)
Smoothed 2D Supervision stabilizes joint optimization of camera poses and scene representations by blurring 2D training images with a scheduled set of 2D Gaussian kernels. It solves the problem of noisy, high-frequency gradients that destabilize camera alignment. It sets itself apart from [Frequency Regularization](6130-frequency-regularization.md) by using a handcrafted, progressive reduction of blur variance rather than frequency analysis. Choose this when camera pose optimization is unstable or spectral inconsistencies arise.

### [3D Half-Gaussian Splatting Covariance Transformation and Regularization](9150-3d-half-gaussian-splatting-covariance-transformation-and-reg.md)
This method regularizes 3D Gaussian kernels into "half-Gaussians" by transforming their covariance matrices to align with local surface normals, effectively modeling sharp transitions between object surfaces and empty space. It sets itself apart from [Geometry Regularization](14222-geometry-regularization.md) by explicitly enforcing a planar cut in the covariance structure rather than just penalizing geometric deviations, resulting in kernels that behave like surfels. Choose this when surface sharpness and precise boundary modeling are critical.

### [Hard and Soft Depth Regularization](9178-hard-and-soft-depth-regularization.md)
Hard and Soft Depth Regularization prevents detail loss and blurred appearance by constraining geometry through the movement of Gaussian centers rather than deforming Gaussian shapes. It solves the problem where standard depth regularization forces anisotropic Gaussians to fit smooth monocular depth estimates, creating a geometry conflict with complex color appearance. It sets itself apart from [Frequency Regularization](6130-frequency-regularization.md) by focusing on spatial reshaping of primitives, and from [Smoothed 2D Supervision](7213-smoothed-2d-supervision.md) by explicitly decoupling the optimization of position and opacity via two distinct depth renders. Choose this when monocular depth priors are available and detail preservation is required.

### [Cross-scale geometric adaptation](10796-cross-scale-geometric-adaptation.md)
Cross-scale geometric adaptation is a self-adaptive regularization method that uses reprojection errors across multiple voxel scales to guide geometry learning without complex scheduling or explicit depth ground truth. It selects render depths with minimal reprojection error across different scales as pseudo labels, ensuring geometric integrity by leveraging low-frequency components from low-resolution voxels for coarse geometry early in training, while medium- and high-resolution voxels refine details as training advances. It sets itself apart from siblings like [Hard and Soft Depth Regularization](9178-hard-and-soft-depth-regularization.md) by avoiding scale mismatches inherent in single-scale depth priors, providing a stronger and more robust constraint that significantly reduces floaters and improves convergence quality. Choose this when multi-view consistency is available but explicit depth maps are not.

### [Geometry Regularization](14222-geometry-regularization.md)
Geometry regularization improves the geometric coherence and smoothness of 3D Gaussian Splatting models by constraining the shape and orientation of the Gaussians, distinct from depth supervision which only constrains their 3D location. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Hard and Soft Depth Regularization](9178-hard-and-soft-depth-regularization.md) by focusing on surface alignment and anisotropy rather than positional depth errors, and from [Frequency Regularization](6130-frequency-regularization.md) by operating in spatial geometry rather than spectral frequency space. It primarily solves the problem of "floaters" and noisy, blobby geometry by encouraging Gaussians to flatten into surfels aligned with the underlying surface. Choose this when general geometric smoothness and floater reduction are the primary goals.

### Wild-GS
- [S1] A method that aligns pixel appearance features from image triplanes directly to 3D Gaussians and uses depth regularization and visibility maps to mitigate transient effects and constrain geometry.

### Source Feature Extrapolation
- [S2] A technique to improve extrapolation capabilities beyond source view frustums by padding source images and adding positional encoding channels for padded regions, preventing smearing artifacts in regions not visible by source images.
- [S2] Apply border padding to source images $I^{(i)}$.
- [S2] Create a channel $\Gamma$ containing pixel-wise positional encodings for padded regions: $\Gamma[u,v] = \gamma(u,v)$ if $(u,v)$ is not in $I^{(i)}$, else 0. Concatenate $I_{pad}$ and $\Gamma$ to form $I'(i) = \text{concatenate}(I_{pad}, \Gamma)$.
- [S2] $\gamma(\cdot)$ denotes positional encoding with exponential frequencies.

### SDF-Regularized 3DGS
- [S3] Methods to improve geometric fidelity in 3DGS by imposing physical constraints, such as Signed Distance Fields (SDFs), monocular depth priors, or multi-view geometric constraints, during optimization.
- [S3] Introduce a regularization term to minimize the difference between an ideal SDF and the SDF calculated from Gaussians.
- [S3] Use a dual-branch framework with GS- and SDF-branches, jointly optimized to provide mutual guidance.
- [S3] Incorporate geometric regularization such as monocular depth priors or multi-plane Gaussian optimization.

### FreGS
- [S4, unofficial] Applies progressive frequency regularization to primitives to prevent overfitting and high-frequency artifacts during training.

## Background
The problem of "floaters" and unstructured density clouds in 3DGS was identified as a consequence of optimizing solely for photometric loss [S1, S2]. Early attempts to improve geometry involved integrating Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) or monocular depth priors [S3]. The concept of frequency regularization was introduced to address over-reconstruction by disentangling frequency components [S2]. Smoothed 2D Supervision was developed to stabilize camera pose optimization by restricting the spectrum of the learned scene [S2]. The half-Gaussian approach was proposed to model sharp surface transitions [S1]. Cross-scale adaptation was introduced to leverage multi-view consistency without explicit depth [S1]. These methods collectively form the family of regularization and geometry constraints for 3DGS.
